notes.front: What is the pilot in command (PIC)?
notes.back: The person with final authority and responsibility for the flight, designated as pilot in command, and holding the appropriate ratings for it.
notes.explanation: The definition has three parts, and all must be true: final authority and responsibility, designation before or during the flight, and the appropriate category, class and type rating where one is needed.
notes.example: Like the captain of a ship: two friends who both hold certificates agree before engine start which of them will be PIC, and that one answers for the flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR), "Pilot in command"
notes.evidence: Pilot in command means the person who: (1) Has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the flight; (2) Has been designated as pilot in command before or during the flight;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a private pilot certificate allow, in one sentence?
notes.back: Flying for noncommercial purposes, with passengers and even in furtherance of a business, but without being paid for services as a pilot.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it almost unlimited authority to fly under VFR; the main limit is on being compensated as a pilot.
notes.example: Like a full driving licence without a taxi licence: you may drive friends to the coast, but you may not charge them a fare for driving.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 1, "Private Pilot"
notes.evidence: gives almost unlimited authority to fly under VFR. Passengers may be carried and flight in furtherance of a business is permitted; however, a private pilot may not be compensated in any way for services as a pilot

notes.front: What is a student pilot certificate for?
notes.back: It allows a person being trained by a flight instructor to fly alone (solo), under specific, limited circumstances.
notes.explanation: The solo privileges are limited: the rules later in this topic set out those limits and the endorsements they depend on.
notes.example: Like a provisional driving licence: the learner may drive on the road, but only on the conditions attached to it.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 1, "Student Pilot Certificate"
notes.evidence: alone (solo) under specific, limited circumstances and must

notes.front: For pilot certification, what are a category and a class?
notes.back: Category: a broad classification of aircraft (such as airplane). Class: aircraft within a category with similar operating characteristics (such as single-engine land).
notes.explanation: Class sits inside category: the handbook quotes these definitions from part 1, section 1.1, where a class is a grouping within a category.
notes.example: Like "vehicle" and "motorcycle" on a driving licence: the rating "airplane single-engine land" names the category (airplane) and the class (single-engine land).
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 1, "Aircraft Classifications" (definitions from 14 CFR 1.1)
notes.evidence: classification of aircraft within a category having similar operating characteristics

notes.front: In pilot training, what is an endorsement?
notes.back: A written, signed statement, usually by a certificated flight instructor, that the holder has received training in specific skill areas.
notes.explanation: The signature is what matters: the handbook says endorsements are written and signed by an authorised individual, usually a certificated flight instructor.
notes.example: Like a teacher signing a lab book to say a pupil may now use the equipment unsupervised.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 1, "Pilot Certifications"
notes.evidence: that the certificate holder has received training in specific skill areas. Endorsements are written and signed by an authorized individual, usually a certificated flight instructor

notes.front: Who counts as an authorized instructor under part 61?
notes.back: A holder of a part 61 ground or flight instructor certificate, giving training within the privileges and limitations of that certificate.
notes.explanation: A ground instructor counts only for ground training; a flight instructor counts for ground or flight training, each within the limits of their own certificate.
notes.example: Like a driving instructor who may teach on the road, while a classroom tutor may only teach the theory.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.1 Applicability and definitions (eCFR), paragraph (b), "Authorized instructor"
notes.evidence: when conducting ground training in accordance with the privileges and limitations of his or her ground instructor certificate; (ii) A person who holds a flight instructor certificate issued under part 61 of this chapter and is in compliance with § 61.197, when conducting ground training or flight training
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a medical certificate, and which class does a private pilot need at least?
notes.back: The part 67 certificate of medical fitness; exercising private pilot privileges needs at least a third-class one, except under the § 61.113(i) conditions.
notes.explanation: The exception refers to the conditions of § 61.113(i), which the next card introduces as BasicMed.
notes.example: Like a fitness-to-drive certificate for a lorry driver: the licence is useless without it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (a)(3)(i)
notes.evidence: Must hold at least a third-class medical certificate— (i) When exercising the privileges of a private pilot certificate, recreational pilot certificate, or student pilot certificate, except when operating under the conditions and limitations set forth in § 61.113(i)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is BasicMed?
notes.back: The part 68 alternative: a pilot may fly under § 61.113(i) without a part 67 medical certificate, by meeting medical education and examination requirements.
notes.explanation: Part 68 sets out the course and the examination that replace the medical certificate for these flights; the conditions and limits come in the cards that follow.
notes.example: Like renewing a sports club membership through your own doctor and an education module, instead of a formal examination at the club.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 68.1 Applicability (eCFR)
notes.evidence: This part prescribes the medical education and examination requirements for operating an aircraft under § 61.113(i) of this chapter without holding a medical certificate issued under part 67
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the minimum age for a private pilot certificate with an airplane rating?
notes.back: 17 years.
notes.explanation: The rule sets 17 for any rating other than glider or balloon.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.103 Eligibility requirements: General (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Be at least 17 years of age for a rating in other than a glider or balloon.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the minimum age for a student pilot certificate for aeroplanes?
notes.back: 16 years.
notes.explanation: The rule sets 16 for anything other than a glider or balloon.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.83 Eligibility requirements for student pilots (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Be at least 16 years of age for other than the operation of a glider or balloon.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the minimum age to take the Private Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.back: 15 years.
notes.explanation: The testing matrix lists the minimum age for each knowledge test.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (25 September 2026), private pilot tests table
notes.evidence: Private Pilot Airplane 60 15 2.0 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much time is allowed for the Private Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.back: 2.0 hours.
notes.explanation: The testing matrix dated 25 September 2026 lists 2.0 hours as the allotted time for this test.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (25 September 2026), private pilot tests table
notes.evidence: Private Pilot Airplane 60 15 2.0 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many questions are on the Private Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.back: 60 questions.
notes.explanation: The testing matrix lists 60 questions for this test.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (25 September 2026), private pilot tests table
notes.evidence: Private Pilot Airplane 60 15 2.0 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the passing score for the Private Pilot Airplane knowledge test?
notes.back: 70 (per cent).
notes.explanation: The testing matrix lists 70 as the passing score for this test.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (25 September 2026), private pilot tests table
notes.evidence: Private Pilot Airplane 60 15 2.0 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What language requirement must an applicant for a private pilot certificate meet?
notes.back: Be able to read, speak, write and understand the English language.
notes.explanation: If a medical reason prevents one of these, the Administrator may put operating limitations on the certificate instead.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.103 Eligibility requirements: General (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: Be able to read, speak, write, and understand the English language. If the applicant is unable to meet one of these requirements due to medical reasons, then the Administrator may place such operating limitations
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Before the private pilot knowledge test, what must an applicant receive from an authorized instructor?
notes.back: A logbook endorsement certifying the person is prepared for the knowledge test, after training or a review of home study.
notes.explanation: The instructor must either have given the training or reviewed the home study on the § 61.105(b) knowledge areas.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.103 Eligibility requirements: General (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: Receive a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who: (1) Conducted the training or reviewed the person's home study on the aeronautical knowledge areas
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Before the private pilot practical test, what must an applicant receive from an authorized instructor?
notes.back: Flight training and a logbook endorsement certifying the person is prepared for the practical test.
notes.explanation: The endorsing instructor must be the one who conducted the training in the areas of operation for the rating sought.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.103 Eligibility requirements: General (eCFR), paragraph (f)
notes.evidence: Receive flight training and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who: (1) Conducted the training in the areas of operation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For a private pilot certificate with airplane single-engine rating, how much flight time must be logged in total?
notes.back: At least 40 hours.
notes.explanation: The 40 hours must include set amounts of instruction and solo flight, taught in the next cards.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: must log at least 40 hours of flight time that includes at least 20 hours of flight training from an authorized instructor and 10 hours of solo flight training
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Of the 40 hours for a private pilot airplane single-engine rating, how many must be flight training from an authorized instructor?
notes.back: At least 20 hours.
notes.explanation: The rest of the minimum is made up of solo and other flight time.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: must log at least 40 hours of flight time that includes at least 20 hours of flight training from an authorized instructor
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Of the 40 hours for a private pilot airplane single-engine rating, how many must be solo flight?
notes.back: At least 10 hours.
notes.explanation: The 10 solo hours have their own required content: solo cross-country time and towered-airport landings.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)(5)
notes.evidence: 10 hours of solo flight time in a single-engine airplane, consisting of at least— (i) 5 hours of solo cross-country time;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What long solo cross-country flight does the private pilot airplane single-engine rating require?
notes.back: One of 150 NM total, with full-stop landings at three points and one leg of more than 50 NM straight-line.
notes.explanation: The rule sets a total distance, three landing points and one long leg.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)(5)(ii)
notes.evidence: One solo cross country flight of 150 nautical miles total distance, with full-stop landings at three points, and one segment of the flight consisting of a straight-line distance of more than 50 nautical miles
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Within what period before the practical test must the 3 hours of test-preparation training be flown?
notes.back: Within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test.
notes.explanation: The window is counted in calendar months back from the month of the test.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)(4)
notes.evidence: 3 hours of flight training with an authorized instructor in a single-engine airplane in preparation for the practical test, which must have been performed within the preceding 2 calendar months from the month of the test
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much night flight training does the private pilot airplane single-engine rating require?
notes.back: At least 3 hours, in a single-engine airplane.
notes.explanation: The night training has two required parts: a cross-country flight and a set of full-stop landings.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: 3 hours of night flight training in a single-engine airplane that includes— (i) One cross-country flight of over 100 nautical miles total distance
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many night takeoffs and landings must the private pilot night training include?
notes.back: 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop, each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern.
notes.explanation: All must be to a full stop at an airport, as part of the 3 hours of night training.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)(ii)
notes.evidence: 10 takeoffs and 10 landings to a full stop (with each landing involving a flight in the traffic pattern) at an airport.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which private pilot knowledge area concerns the National Transportation Safety Board?
notes.back: Its accident reporting requirements.
notes.explanation: It is one of the § 61.105(b) knowledge areas the knowledge test covers.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.105 Aeronautical knowledge (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: Accident reporting requirements of the National Transportation Safety Board;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are two things the "preflight action" knowledge area says a private pilot must know how to obtain or plan?
notes.back: Any two of: runway lengths; takeoff and landing distances; weather reports and forecasts; fuel requirements; alternatives if the flight cannot be completed.
notes.explanation: The area lists information to gather and a plan for alternatives if delays are encountered.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.105 Aeronautical knowledge (eCFR), paragraph (b)(13)
notes.evidence: How to obtain information on runway lengths at airports of intended use, data on takeoff and landing distances, weather reports and forecasts, and fuel requirements; and (ii) How to plan for alternatives
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What endorsement must a student pilot have before any solo flight?
notes.back: A logbook endorsement for the specific make and model, by an authorized instructor who gave the training within the preceding 90 days.
notes.explanation: The endorsement is tied both to a make and model and to recent training.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.87 Solo requirements for student pilots (eCFR), paragraph (n)
notes.evidence: A student pilot may not operate an aircraft in solo flight unless that student pilot has received an endorsement in the student's logbook for the specific make and model aircraft to be flown by an authorized instructor who gave the training within the 90 days preceding the date of the flight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does a student’s solo endorsement stay current?
notes.back: An authorized instructor updates the student’s logbook every 90 days.
notes.explanation: The endorsement remains current for solo flight privileges only while these 90-day updates continue.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.87 Solo requirements for student pilots (eCFR), paragraph (p)(4)
notes.evidence: that endorsement remains current for solo flight privileges, provided an authorized instructor updates the student's logbook every 90 days thereafter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Who gives a student pilot’s pre-solo knowledge test, and what must happen after it?
notes.back: The student’s authorized instructor gives it, and reviews all incorrect answers with the student before authorising solo flight.
notes.explanation: Reviewing the wrong answers comes before the instructor authorises the solo flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.87 Solo requirements for student pilots (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: The student's authorized instructor must— (i) Administer the test; and (ii) At the conclusion of the test, review all incorrect answers with the student before authorizing that student to conduct a solo flight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Beyond what distance from the airport of origin must a student meet the solo cross-country requirements?
notes.back: Any flight greater than 25 NM from the airport where the flight originated (or any solo cross-country flight).
notes.explanation: Landing solo anywhere other than the airport of origin also triggers the requirements.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.93 Solo cross-country flight requirements (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: Conducting a solo cross-country flight, or any flight greater than 25 nautical miles from the airport from where the flight originated.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May a student pilot act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying a passenger?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Carrying a passenger is the first item in the list of student pilot limitations.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.89 General limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: A student pilot may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft: (1) That is carrying a passenger;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are three commercial limits on a student pilot acting as pilot in command?
notes.back: Not carrying property for compensation or hire; not for compensation or hire; not in furtherance of a business.
notes.explanation: All three are in the same list of student limitations.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.89 General limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)–(4)
notes.evidence: (2) That is carrying property for compensation or hire; (3) For compensation or hire; (4) In furtherance of a business;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Below what flight or surface visibility may a student pilot not act as pilot in command?
notes.back: Less than 3 statute miles by day, or 5 statute miles at night.
notes.explanation: A student also may not fly when the flight cannot be made with visual reference to the surface.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.89 General limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(6)–(7)
notes.evidence: With a flight or surface visibility of less than 3 statute miles during daylight hours or 5 statute miles at night; (7) When the flight cannot be made with visual reference to the surface;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the general rule on a private pilot and compensation?
notes.back: No acting as pilot in command for compensation or hire, or of an aircraft carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire.
notes.explanation: Paragraphs (b) to (h) of the same section then list the only exceptions.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (h) of this section, no person who holds a private pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of an aircraft that is carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire; nor may that person, for compensation or hire, act as pilot in command of an aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When may a private pilot act as pilot in command in connection with a business or employment?
notes.back: When the flight is only incidental to that business or employment, and carries no passengers or property for compensation or hire.
notes.explanation: Both conditions must hold at once.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: (1) The flight is only incidental to that business or employment; and (2) The aircraft does not carry passengers or property for compensation or hire.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With passengers on board, what share of the flight’s operating expenses must a private pilot pay?
notes.back: Not less than the pro rata share.
notes.explanation: Sharing is allowed only for fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For search and location operations, what may a private pilot be reimbursed for?
notes.back: Aircraft operating expenses directly related to the operation: only fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees.
notes.explanation: Reimbursement is limited to the same four kinds of expense as pro rata sharing.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: A private pilot may be reimbursed for aircraft operating expenses that are directly related to search and location operations, provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much logged flight time does a private pilot who is an aircraft salesman need to demonstrate an aircraft to a prospective buyer?
notes.back: At least 200 hours.
notes.explanation: The exception is narrow: it covers a salesman demonstrating an aircraft in flight to someone who may buy it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (f)
notes.evidence: A private pilot who is an aircraft salesman and who has at least 200 hours of logged flight time may demonstrate an aircraft in flight to a prospective buyer.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which certificate’s privileges, in an aircraft other than a balloon or glider, need at least a second-class medical certificate?
notes.back: A commercial pilot certificate.
notes.explanation: The rule covers commercial privileges except in a balloon or glider.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)(ii)
notes.evidence: Privileges of a commercial pilot certificate in an aircraft other than a balloon or glider;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For private pilot privileges, when does a third-class medical expire if the pilot was under 40 at the examination?
notes.back: At the end of the last day of the 60th month after the month of the examination.
notes.explanation: The rule counts whole months from the month of the examination shown on the certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)(3)(i)
notes.evidence: a sport pilot certificate (when not using a U.S. driver's license as medical qualification) 60th month after the month of the date of examination shown on the medical certificate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For private pilot privileges, when does a third-class medical expire if the pilot was 40 or older at the examination?
notes.back: At the end of the last day of the 24th month after the month of the examination.
notes.explanation: The table counts whole months from the month of the examination shown on the certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)(3)(ii)
notes.evidence: a sport pilot certificate (when not using a U.S. driver's license as medical qualification) 24th month after the month of the date of examination shown on the medical certificate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which age decides whether a medical certificate lasts 60 or 24 months for private privileges?
notes.back: The pilot’s age on the date of the examination for the most recent medical certificate.
notes.explanation: The table asks how old you were "on the date of examination", not how old you are when you fly.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: And on the date ofexamination for your most recent medical certificate you were
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, how many occupants may the aircraft be authorised to carry?
notes.back: Not more than 7 occupants.
notes.explanation: This is a limit on the aircraft’s authorisation, separate from the limit on passengers actually on board.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(1)
notes.evidence: The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, what is the maximum takeoff weight limit of the aircraft?
notes.back: Not more than 12,500 pounds.
notes.explanation: It is one of the aircraft conditions in § 61.113(i)(1).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(1)
notes.evidence: has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, how many passengers may be on board?
notes.back: No more than 6 passengers.
notes.explanation: The aircraft may be authorised for up to 7 occupants, but no more than 6 of those on board may be passengers.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(1)
notes.evidence: is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, above what altitude may no part of the flight be carried out?
notes.back: More than 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: The limit applies to each portion of the flight, not just the cruise.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: The flight, including each portion of the flight, is not carried out— (i) At an altitude that is more than 18,000 feet above mean sea level;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, what indicated airspeed may no part of the flight exceed?
notes.back: 250 knots.
notes.explanation: It sits in the same list of flight conditions as the altitude and country limits.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(2)(iii)
notes.evidence: At an indicated airspeed exceeding 250 knots
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, may the flight go outside the United States?
notes.back: Only if authorised by the country in which the flight is conducted.
notes.explanation: The rule forbids flight outside the United States unless the other country authorises it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(2)(ii)
notes.evidence: Outside the United States unless authorized by the country in which the flight is conducted
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What kind of licence must a pilot hold to fly under BasicMed?
notes.back: A valid U.S. driver’s licence.
notes.explanation: The driver’s licence is one of the entry conditions of § 61.113(i), with the § 61.23(c)(3) requirements.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)
notes.evidence: without holding a medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter provided the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets the requirements of § 61.23(c)(3)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, within what period must the medical education course have been completed?
notes.back: During the 24 calendar months before acting as pilot in command.
notes.explanation: The pilot must also keep the certificate of course completion.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(i)(C)
notes.evidence: Complete the medical education course set forth in § 68.3 of this chapter during the 24 calendar months before acting as pilot in command or serving as a required flightcrew member in an operation conducted under § 61.113(i) and retain a certification of course completion
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under BasicMed, within what period must the comprehensive medical examination have been received, and from whom?
notes.back: During the 48 calendar months before acting as pilot in command, from a State-licensed physician.
notes.explanation: The examination is conducted in accordance with the requirements of part 68.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(i)(D)
notes.evidence: Receive a comprehensive medical examination from a State-licensed physician during the 48 calendar months before acting as pilot in command or serving as a required flightcrew member of an operation conducted under § 61.113(i) and that medical examination is conducted in accordance with the requirements in part 68
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What earlier medical certificate must a BasicMed pilot have held?
notes.back: A part 67 medical certificate held at any point after July 14, 2006.
notes.explanation: Having held one at any point after that date is enough.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(i)(B)
notes.evidence: At any point after July 14, 2006, have held a medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For BasicMed, may the pilot’s most recently issued medical certificate be expired?
notes.back: Yes. It may be expired, but it cannot have been suspended or revoked.
notes.explanation: It may also include an authorisation for special issuance.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(ii)
notes.evidence: The most recently issued medical certificate— (A) May include an authorization for special issuance; (B) May be expired; and (C) Cannot have been suspended or revoked.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which two BasicMed documents must the pilot have available in the logbook?
notes.back: The completed medical examination checklist (§ 68.7) and the certificate of course completion.
notes.explanation: These are the records that show the examination and the course were done.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(3)
notes.evidence: The pilot has available in his or her logbook— (i) The completed medical examination checklist required under § 68.7 of this chapter; and (ii) The certificate of course completion
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When may a holder of a medical certificate not act as pilot in command?
notes.back: While knowing, or having reason to know, of a medical condition that would make them unable to meet the requirements for that medical certificate.
notes.explanation: The same bar applies while taking medication or treatment that has that effect.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.53 Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Knows or has reason to know of any medical condition that would make the person unable to meet the requirements for the medical certificate necessary for the pilot operation; or (2) Is taking medication or receiving other treatment
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the minimum length of a flight review, and what must it review?
notes.back: 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training, covering the part 91 rules and chosen maneuvers and procedures.
notes.explanation: The ground hour includes a review of the part 91 general operating and flight rules.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.56 Flight review (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: a flight review consists of a minimum of 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training. The review must include: (1) A review of the current general operating and flight rules of part 91
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How recent must a flight review be for a pilot to act as pilot in command?
notes.back: Since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which the pilot acts as pilot in command.
notes.explanation: The count is in calendar months, so a review done any day in a month lasts to the end of that month two years on.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.56 Flight review (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: no person may act as pilot in command of an aircraft unless, since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which that pilot acts as pilot in command
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What can stand in for a flight review within the same period?
notes.back: Passing a pilot proficiency check or practical test for a pilot certificate, rating or operating privilege, among others.
notes.explanation: The rule lists checks by an examiner, an approved check airman or a U.S. Armed Force.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.56 Flight review (eCFR), paragraph (d)(1)
notes.evidence: A pilot proficiency check or practical test conducted by an examiner, an approved pilot check airman, or a U.S. Armed Force, for a pilot certificate, rating, or operating privilege.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What recent experience must a pilot have to act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying persons?
notes.back: Three takeoffs and three landings within 90 days, as sole manipulator, in the same category and class, and type if a type rating is required.
notes.explanation: The same rule applies to any aircraft certificated for more than one pilot flight crewmember.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: no person may act as a pilot in command of an aircraft carrying persons or of an aircraft certificated for more than one pilot flight crewmember unless that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For a tailwheel aeroplane, what extra condition applies to the three takeoffs and landings?
notes.back: They must be made to a full stop, in an airplane with a tailwheel.
notes.explanation: The full-stop condition is written for aeroplanes with a tailwheel.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)(ii)
notes.evidence: if the aircraft to be flown is an airplane with a tailwheel, the takeoffs and landings must have been made to a full stop in an airplane with a tailwheel.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What night recent experience must a pilot have to carry persons at night?
notes.back: Three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop within the preceding 90 days, between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise.
notes.explanation: The requirement applies to carrying persons during that same period of the night.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: unless within the preceding 90 days that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which flight time must a pilot record in a logbook?
notes.back: Training and experience used for a certificate, rating or flight review, and experience used for recent flight experience.
notes.explanation: These are the two kinds of time the rule requires to be documented and recorded.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.51 Pilot logbooks (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Training and aeronautical experience used to meet the requirements for a certificate, rating, or flight review of this part. (2) The aeronautical experience required for meeting the recent flight experience requirements
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a reasonable request, which three kinds of official may ask a pilot to present the pilot certificate, medical certificate and logbook?
notes.back: The Administrator (the FAA), an authorised representative of the NTSB, and any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer.
notes.explanation: The rule covers any other record required by part 61 as well.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.51 Pilot logbooks (eCFR), paragraph (i)(1)
notes.evidence: Persons must present their pilot certificate, medical certificate, logbook, or any other record required by this part for inspection upon a reasonable request by— (i) The Administrator; (ii) An authorized representative from the National Transportation Safety Board
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Where must a pilot’s certificate be when exercising its privileges?
notes.back: In the pilot’s physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: Readily accessible in the aircraft is enough; it need not be on the pilot’s person.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.3 Requirement for certificates, ratings, privileges, and authorizations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: Has in the person's physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft when exercising the privileges of that pilot certificate or authorization— (i) A pilot certificate issued under this part
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides the pilot certificate, what identification must a pilot have when exercising its privileges?
notes.back: A photo identification, such as a driver’s licence issued by a State, in their possession or readily accessible in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: A driver’s licence is the first of the acceptable forms the rule lists.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.3 Requirement for certificates, ratings, privileges, and authorizations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Has a photo identification that is in that person's physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft when exercising the privileges of that pilot certificate or authorization. The photo identification must be a: (i) Driver's license issued by a State
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What medical document must a required pilot flight crewmember have with them?
notes.back: The appropriate part 67 medical certificate, or other documentation acceptable to the FAA, in physical possession or readily accessible.
notes.explanation: The rule allows other documentation acceptable to the FAA as an alternative to the part 67 certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.3 Requirement for certificates, ratings, privileges, and authorizations (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: holds the appropriate medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter, or other documentation acceptable to the FAA, that is in that person's physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Do private and student pilot certificates issued today have an expiration date?
notes.back: No. Pilot certificates, including student certificates issued after April 1, 2016, are issued without an expiration date.
notes.explanation: For student certificates the issue date matters: those issued after April 1, 2016 have no expiration date.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.19 Duration of pilot and instructor certificates and privileges (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: A pilot certificate (including a student pilot certificate issued after April 1, 2016) issued under this part is issued without an expiration date.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After a change of permanent mailing address, how long may a pilot exercise certificate privileges without notifying the FAA?
notes.back: 30 days.
notes.explanation: The notice to the FAA must be in writing.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.60 Change of address (eCFR)
notes.evidence: who has made a change in permanent mailing address may not, after 30 days from that date, exercise the privileges of the certificate unless the holder has notified in writing the FAA
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What may follow a conviction under a drug statute for a part 61 applicant or holder?
notes.back: Denial of an application for up to 1 year after the final conviction, or suspension or revocation of any certificate.
notes.explanation: The rule makes such a conviction grounds for these actions.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.15 Offenses involving alcohol or drugs (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: depressant or stimulant drugs or substances is grounds for: (1) Denial of an application for any certificate, rating, or authorization issued under this part for a period of up to 1 year after the date of final conviction; or (2) Suspension or revocation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Within how many days must a pilot send the FAA a written report of a motor vehicle action?
notes.back: Not later than 60 days after the motor vehicle action.
notes.explanation: The report goes to the FAA’s Civil Aviation Security Division.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.15 Offenses involving alcohol or drugs (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: shall provide a written report of each motor vehicle action to the FAA, Civil Aviation Security Division (AMC-700), P.O. Box 25810, Oklahoma City, OK 73125, not later than 60 days after the motor vehicle action.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What counts as a "motor vehicle action" under § 61.15?
notes.back: A conviction, or loss or denial of a driving licence, for driving while intoxicated, impaired or under the influence of alcohol or a drug.
notes.explanation: Each must have occurred after November 29, 1990.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.15 Offenses involving alcohol or drugs (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: A conviction after November 29, 1990, for the violation of any Federal or State statute relating to the operation of a motor vehicle while intoxicated by alcohol or a drug
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What makes an aeroplane a "complex airplane"?
notes.back: Retractable landing gear, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller.
notes.explanation: An engine control system with a digital computer, such as a full authority digital engine control, also counts.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.1 Applicability and definitions (eCFR), paragraph (b), "Complex airplane"
notes.evidence: Complex airplane means an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller, including airplanes equipped with an engine control system consisting of a digital computer and associated accessories for controlling the engine and propeller, such as a full authority digital engine control
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must a pilot have before acting as pilot in command of a complex airplane?
notes.back: Ground and flight training from an authorized instructor, and a one-time logbook endorsement of proficiency.
notes.explanation: The instructor certifies proficiency once, in a one-time endorsement.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: Received a one-time endorsement in the pilot's logbook from an authorized instructor who certifies the person is proficient to operate a complex airplane.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a high-performance airplane?
notes.back: An aeroplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower.
notes.explanation: The definition sits inside the endorsement rule itself.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (f)
notes.evidence: a high-performance airplane (an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must a pilot have before acting as pilot in command of a high-performance airplane?
notes.back: Ground and flight training from an authorized instructor, and a one-time logbook endorsement of proficiency.
notes.explanation: It follows the same pattern as the complex airplane endorsement.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (f)
notes.evidence: Received and logged ground and flight training from an authorized instructor in a high-performance airplane
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must a pilot have before acting as pilot in command of a tailwheel aeroplane?
notes.back: Flight training in a tailwheel aeroplane from an authorized instructor, and a logbook endorsement of proficiency.
notes.explanation: Both the logged training and the endorsement are needed.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (i)
notes.evidence: no person may act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane unless that person has received and logged flight training from an authorized instructor in a tailwheel airplane and received an endorsement
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which pressurised aircraft need a high-altitude endorsement before a pilot may act as pilot in command?
notes.back: Those with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: The endorsement follows logged ground training from an authorized instructor.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (g)
notes.evidence: no person may act as pilot in command of a pressurized aircraft (an aircraft that has a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL), unless that person has received and logged ground training from an authorized instructor and obtained an endorsement
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How recently must the knowledge test have been passed to take the private pilot practical test?
notes.back: Within the 24-calendar-month period before the month in which the practical test is completed.
notes.explanation: The count is in calendar months, back from the month the practical test is completed.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.39 Prerequisites for practical tests (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: Within the 24-calendar-month period preceding the month the applicant completes the practical test, if a knowledge test is required
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does an applicant need before retaking a failed knowledge or practical test?
notes.back: The necessary training from an authorized instructor, and an endorsement from the instructor who gave that training.
notes.explanation: The instructor must have determined that the applicant is proficient to pass the test.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.49 Retesting after failure (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: The necessary training from an authorized instructor who has determined that the applicant is proficient to pass the test; and (2) An endorsement from an authorized instructor who gave the applicant the additional training.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Two certificated pilots fly together. Before takeoff they agree that Sam will be pilot in command, and Sam holds the right ratings. Who has final authority for the flight?
notes.back: Sam, the designated pilot in command.
notes.explanation: Final authority and responsibility belong to the person designated as pilot in command who holds the appropriate ratings.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (eCFR), "Pilot in command"
notes.evidence: Has been designated as pilot in command before or during the flight; and (3) Holds the appropriate category, class, and type rating, if appropriate, for the conduct of the flight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A 16-year-old has all the hours and has passed every test for a private pilot certificate with an airplane rating. Can the certificate be issued?
notes.back: No. The minimum age for an airplane rating is 17.
notes.explanation: Only glider and balloon ratings allow the certificate at 16.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.103 Eligibility requirements: General (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Be at least 17 years of age for a rating in other than a glider or balloon.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A 15-year-old wants a student pilot certificate to fly an aeroplane solo. Is she eligible?
notes.back: Not yet. For aeroplanes the minimum age is 16.
notes.explanation: The age of 14 applies only to gliders and balloons.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.83 Eligibility requirements for student pilots (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Be at least 16 years of age for other than the operation of a glider or balloon.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A candidate plans to spend two and a half hours on the Private Pilot Airplane knowledge test. Is that time available?
notes.back: No. The testing matrix allows 2.0 hours for this test.
notes.explanation: The testing matrix is the document that lists the allotted time for each test.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (25 September 2026), private pilot tests table
notes.evidence: Private Pilot Airplane 60 15 2.0 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Because of a medical condition, an applicant cannot speak but reads, writes and understands English. What may the Administrator do?
notes.back: Place operating limitations on the certificate as necessary for safe operation of the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The rule provides for limitations when one of the language requirements cannot be met for medical reasons.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.103 Eligibility requirements: General (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: If the applicant is unable to meet one of these requirements due to medical reasons, then the Administrator may place such operating limitations on that applicant's pilot certificate as are necessary for the safe operation of the aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An applicant for the airplane single-engine rating has 45 hours in total: 27 with an instructor and 8 solo. Has she met the minimums?
notes.back: No. She has enough total and dual time but needs at least 10 hours of solo flight.
notes.explanation: The 40 hours must include at least 20 hours of training and 10 hours of solo.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.109 Aeronautical experience (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: must log at least 40 hours of flight time that includes at least 20 hours of flight training from an authorized instructor and 10 hours of solo flight training
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A student’s last solo endorsement for a trainer was made 100 days ago, and nobody has updated it since. May she fly it solo today?
notes.back: No. The endorsement must be updated by an authorized instructor every 90 days.
notes.explanation: Solo privileges depend on an endorsement for the make and model that is kept current every 90 days.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.87 Solo requirements for student pilots (eCFR), paragraph (p)(4)
notes.evidence: that endorsement remains current for solo flight privileges, provided an authorized instructor updates the student's logbook every 90 days thereafter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A student pilot with a valid solo endorsement is asked by a friend for a short local flight. May the student take the friend?
notes.back: No. A student pilot may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying a passenger.
notes.explanation: The solo endorsement does not change the student pilot limitations.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.89 General limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: A student pilot may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft: (1) That is carrying a passenger;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At night, a student pilot on a solo flight sees reported visibility of 4 statute miles. May the flight go ahead?
notes.back: No. At night a student pilot needs at least 5 statute miles of flight or surface visibility.
notes.explanation: The daytime minimum of 3 miles does not apply at night.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.89 General limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(6)
notes.evidence: With a flight or surface visibility of less than 3 statute miles during daylight hours or 5 statute miles at night;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot is offered a fee to fly a stranger’s aeroplane to another city, with no one else on board. May he accept?
notes.back: No. A private pilot may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft for compensation or hire.
notes.explanation: The ban covers being paid to fly, not only carrying paying passengers or property.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: nor may that person, for compensation or hire, act as pilot in command of an aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A surveyor who holds a private pilot certificate flies herself to a site visit for her employer, alone. Is that allowed?
notes.back: Yes, if the flight is only incidental to her job and carries no passengers or property for hire.
notes.explanation: Her pay is for the survey work; the flight is incidental to that employment.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: A private pilot may, for compensation or hire, act as pilot in command of an aircraft in connection with any business or employment if: (1) The flight is only incidental to that business or employment
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot and three passengers share a flight whose fuel and rental cost 400 dollars in total. What is the least the pilot may pay?
notes.back: 100 dollars, the pilot’s pro rata (one-in-four) share.
notes.explanation: A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of those expenses.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: A private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses of a flight with passengers
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which of these costs may a private pilot share pro rata with passengers?
notes.back: A) Aircraft rental fees.
notes.choices:
A) Aircraft rental fees
B) A fee for the pilot’s time
C) The pilot’s annual flying club membership
notes.choicesExplained: B: paying the pilot for their time is compensation, which the rule forbids. C: the list covers only fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees, not the pilot’s own fixed costs.
notes.explanation: The sharing rule covers only fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: provided the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, or rental fees.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot holds a first-class medical certificate. May it be used for private pilot privileges?
notes.back: Yes. Private privileges need "at least" a third-class certificate, so a higher class also qualifies.
notes.explanation: The rule sets a minimum class, not an exact one.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (a)(3)(i)
notes.evidence: Must hold at least a third-class medical certificate— (i) When exercising the privileges of a private pilot certificate
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot aged 35 had a third-class medical examination on 10 March 2024. Until when may she use it for private privileges?
notes.back: Until the end of 31 March 2029 (the end of the 60th month after March 2024).
notes.explanation: She was under 40 on the date of the examination, so the 60-month period applies.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)(3)(i)
notes.evidence: 60th month after the month of the date of examination shown on the medical certificate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot aged 52 had a third-class medical examination on 15 June 2025. Until when may he use it for private privileges?
notes.back: Until the end of 30 June 2027 (the end of the 24th month after June 2025).
notes.explanation: He was 40 or older on the date of the examination, so the 24-month period applies.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)(3)(ii)
notes.evidence: 24th month after the month of the date of examination shown on the medical certificate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot was 39 at her third-class medical examination and turns 40 the following month. Does her certificate now last only 24 months?
notes.back: No. Her age on the date of the examination (39) decides it, so it still lasts 60 months.
notes.explanation: The duration table looks at age on the date of examination for the most recent medical certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: And on the date ofexamination for your most recent medical certificate you were
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A BasicMed pilot wants to fly a 10-seat aeroplane with a maximum takeoff weight of 12,000 pounds. Is it allowed?
notes.back: No. Under BasicMed the aircraft may be authorised to carry not more than 7 occupants.
notes.explanation: The aircraft must meet every condition: the weight is within 12,500 pounds, but the seating is not.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(1)
notes.evidence: The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A BasicMed pilot flying a turbocharged aeroplane wants to climb to 19,000 feet MSL to top the weather. May he?
notes.back: No. Under BasicMed no part of the flight may be above 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: The limit covers each portion of the flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: At an altitude that is more than 18,000 feet above mean sea level;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A BasicMed pilot completed the medical education course 30 calendar months ago and her physician examination 20 months ago. May she act as pilot in command?
notes.back: No. The course must have been completed within the preceding 24 calendar months.
notes.explanation: The examination (48 calendar months) is current, but the course is not.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(i)(C)
notes.evidence: Complete the medical education course set forth in § 68.3 of this chapter during the 24 calendar months before acting as pilot in command
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A new pilot has never held a part 67 medical certificate. Can he use BasicMed straight away?
notes.back: No. BasicMed requires having held a part 67 medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006.
notes.explanation: That earlier certificate may now be expired, but it must have existed.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.23 Medical certificates: Requirement and duration (eCFR), paragraph (c)(3)(i)(B)
notes.evidence: At any point after July 14, 2006, have held a medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot with a current medical certificate starts a medication that, he knows, makes him unable to meet the standards for that certificate. May he act as pilot in command?
notes.back: No. He may not while taking medication that leaves him unable to meet the requirements for the medical certificate.
notes.explanation: The certificate being unexpired does not matter; the bar applies while the deficiency lasts.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.53 Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Is taking medication or receiving other treatment for a medical condition that results in the person being unable to meet the requirements for the medical certificate necessary for the pilot operation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot completed a flight review on 10 May 2024. What is the last day he may act as pilot in command without another?
notes.explanation: In June 2026 the 24th calendar month before is June 2024, so a May 2024 review no longer counts.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.56 Flight review (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month in which that pilot acts as pilot in command
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot’s last three takeoffs and landings were 100 days ago. She wants to take her brother flying today. What must she do first?
notes.back: Make three takeoffs and three landings as sole manipulator of the controls, in the same category and class, without passengers.
notes.explanation: Recent experience is needed only to carry persons, so she may fly solo to regain it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: no person may act as a pilot in command of an aircraft carrying persons or of an aircraft certificated for more than one pilot flight crewmember unless that person has made at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Sunset is at 19:00. A pilot made three full-stop landings between 19:15 and 19:45 last week. Do they count for night passenger-carrying currency?
notes.back: No. Night currency landings must be made between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise.
notes.explanation: Landings before 20:00 fall outside that period, however dark it looks.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After landing, a local police officer reasonably asks to see a pilot’s certificate and logbook. Must the pilot show them?
notes.back: Yes. Any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer may make that request.
notes.explanation: Law enforcement officers are one of the three kinds of official named in the rule.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.51 Pilot logbooks (eCFR), paragraph (i)(1)
notes.evidence: upon a reasonable request by— (i) The Administrator; (ii) An authorized representative from the National Transportation Safety Board; or (iii) Any Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot has her pilot certificate and medical certificate, but left all photo identification at home. May she fly as pilot in command?
notes.back: No. A photo identification must also be in her possession or readily accessible in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The rule requires the certificate and a photo identification together.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.3 Requirement for certificates, ratings, privileges, and authorizations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Has a photo identification that is in that person's physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft when exercising the privileges of that pilot certificate or authorization.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A student pilot certificate was issued in 2019. Has it expired?
notes.back: No. Student pilot certificates issued after April 1, 2016 have no expiration date.
notes.explanation: Only the older paper student certificates expired.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.19 Duration of pilot and instructor certificates and privileges (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: A pilot certificate (including a student pilot certificate issued after April 1, 2016) issued under this part is issued without an expiration date.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot moved house 40 days ago and has not told the FAA. May she fly as pilot in command today?
notes.back: No. After 30 days she may not exercise the privileges until she notifies the FAA in writing.
notes.explanation: The 30-day grace period has passed.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.60 Change of address (eCFR)
notes.evidence: may not, after 30 days from that date, exercise the privileges of the certificate unless the holder has notified in writing the FAA
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot’s driving licence was suspended 45 days ago for driving under the influence of alcohol. What must he do?
notes.back: Send the FAA a written report of the motor vehicle action within 60 days of it, so within the next 15 days.
notes.explanation: A licence suspension for that cause is a motor vehicle action.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.15 Offenses involving alcohol or drugs (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)
notes.evidence: The cancellation, suspension, or revocation of a license to operate a motor vehicle after November 29, 1990, for a cause related to the operation of a motor vehicle while intoxicated by alcohol or a drug
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An aeroplane has retractable landing gear, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller, with a 180 horsepower engine. Which endorsement does a new pilot need to act as pilot in command?
notes.back: A complex airplane endorsement (not a high-performance one, as 180 is not more than 200 horsepower).
notes.explanation: It meets the complex airplane definition, but the high-performance threshold is more than 200 horsepower.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.1 Applicability and definitions (eCFR), paragraph (b), "Complex airplane"
notes.evidence: Complex airplane means an airplane that has a retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A fixed-gear aeroplane has a 230 horsepower engine. Which endorsement does a pilot need to act as pilot in command?
notes.back: A high-performance airplane endorsement.
notes.explanation: More than 200 horsepower makes it high-performance, whatever its landing gear.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (f)
notes.evidence: no person may act as pilot in command of a high-performance airplane (an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower), unless the person has—
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot trained only in nosewheel aeroplanes wants to rent a tailwheel aeroplane. What must she get first?
notes.back: Flight training in a tailwheel aeroplane from an authorized instructor, and a logbook endorsement of proficiency.
notes.explanation: No person may act as pilot in command of a tailwheel aeroplane without both.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.31 Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements (eCFR), paragraph (i)
notes.evidence: no person may act as pilot in command of a tailwheel airplane unless that person has received and logged flight training from an authorized instructor in a tailwheel airplane and received an endorsement
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An applicant passed the knowledge test in March 2024. Can she complete the practical test in April 2026 on that result?
notes.back: No. The test must be passed within the 24 calendar months before the month of the practical test, and March 2024 falls outside.
notes.explanation: For an April 2026 practical test, the window starts in April 2024.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.39 Prerequisites for practical tests (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: Within the 24-calendar-month period preceding the month the applicant completes the practical test
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An applicant fails the practical test in the morning and wants to retake it that afternoon with no further training. Allowed?
notes.back: No. He first needs training from an authorized instructor and an endorsement from that instructor.
notes.explanation: The instructor must have found him proficient to pass the test.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.49 Retesting after failure (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: An applicant for a knowledge or practical test who fails that test may reapply for the test only after the applicant has received:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Is "multiengine" a category or a class?
notes.back: A class (within the airplane category).
notes.explanation: Classes group aircraft within a category by similar operating characteristics; the examples include single engine, multiengine, land and water.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 1, "Aircraft Classifications" (definitions from 14 CFR 1.1)
notes.evidence: Include: single engine; multiengine; land; water;

notes.front: An applicant finished a home-study course and books the private pilot knowledge test without seeing an instructor. What is missing?
notes.back: A logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who reviewed the home study and certified readiness for the test.
notes.explanation: Home study is allowed, but an authorized instructor must review it and endorse the logbook.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.103 Eligibility requirements: General (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: Receive a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor who: (1) Conducted the training or reviewed the person's home study on the aeronautical knowledge areas
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot has a passport but no driver’s licence, and wants to fly under BasicMed. Can he?
notes.back: No. BasicMed requires a valid U.S. driver’s licence.
notes.explanation: The driver’s licence is a condition of flying without a part 67 medical certificate under § 61.113(i).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (i)
notes.evidence: without holding a medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter provided the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does night passenger currency differ from day passenger currency?
notes.back: Night needs three landings to a full stop, between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise; day landings may be touch-and-go (except tailwheel).
notes.explanation: Both count the preceding 90 days, but only the night rule requires full stops in every aeroplane.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many passengers may a recreational pilot carry, compared with a private pilot?
notes.back: A recreational pilot: no more than one; a private pilot: passengers without that limit.
notes.explanation: The recreational certificate is the more restricted one, and it also bars flight in furtherance of a business.
notes.source: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 1, "Recreational Pilot"
notes.evidence: Carry no more than one passenger;

notes.front: Since the 2025 light-sport rule, whom may a sport pilot carry, and which costs may be shared?
notes.back: A passenger, in an aircraft of maximum two occupants, sharing fuel, oil, airport expenses and aircraft rental.
notes.explanation: The handbook addendum rewrote the sport pilot privileges because of the addition of part 61, section 61.316.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-25C Addendum (Modernization of Special Airworthiness Certification rule), 20 October 2025
notes.evidence: Due to the addition of 14 CFR part 61, section 61.316, in the “Privileges” subsection on page 1-16, the second bullet will change to state, “Carry a passenger (maximum two occupants) and share expenses (fuel, oil, airport expenses, and aircraft rental).”

notes.front: May a student pilot, unlike a private pilot, fly in furtherance of a business?
notes.back: No. A student pilot may not act as pilot in command in furtherance of a business; a private pilot may, within § 61.113.
notes.explanation: The student limits are a flat ban; the private rules allow business flights that are only incidental.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.89 General limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(4)
notes.evidence: (3) For compensation or hire; (4) In furtherance of a business;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force
